strengths: The paper identifies a useful vulnerability: feature visualizations can be redirected through weight updates while retaining the deployed architecture. This meaningfully extends the threat model beyond attacks that insert conspicuous computational modules.

The gradient-matching objective and activation-preservation loss are understandable and well motivated. The toy example clearly illustrates how visualization behavior can change away from natural data.

Experiments demonstrate recognizable target manipulations on MNIST and CIFAR-10. The accuracy trade-off, 16 model configurations, multiple similarity metrics, and natural-image retrieval analysis provide useful evidence about the phenomenon.

The limitations and unsuccessful robustness and ImageNet results are reported candidly. This transparency helps establish the method's boundaries. The reported benchmark experiments raise no evident material ethical concerns.
weaknesses: The central claim of minimally changing model behavior is insufficiently supported. At the selected settings, CIFAR-10 accuracy falls from 86.33% to 82.39%, and MNIST accuracy falls from 99.867% to 98.450%. Several model-size experiments incur substantially larger losses. Aggregate accuracy and selected-neuron AUROC also do not establish preservation of individual predictions or internal representations.

The demonstrated scope is narrower than the claims about concealing arbitrary neurons and malicious representations during audits. Experiments manipulate a few output-class neurons; there is no direct evaluation of hidden neurons, backdoor concealment, or an auditing task. These claims require supporting experiments or substantial narrowing.

Targeted manipulation is fragile under relevant visualization settings. Appendix E shows that every evaluated modification removes the MNIST target, while transformation robustness recovers the cat concept on CIFAR-10. The ImageNet example approaches the target after one step but subsequently moves away, and its performance evaluation covers only 20 classes. These results establish a restricted demonstration rather than reliable manipulation across practical visualization procedures.

The convergence analysis does not establish a guarantee for the implemented attack. It assumes a prescribed gradient field, whereas training minimizes errors on finitely sampled points. Lemma A.2 bounds first-step entry into the landing zone but does not establish subsequent invariance or convergence to the target under approximation error; even constant nonzero gradient error shifts the fixed point away from the target.

There are no competing attack baselines or ablations separating the contributions of the slingshot and landing zones. Consequently, the experiments do not establish the advantage of this construction over simpler fine-tuning objectives. Comparing model sizes at a fixed loss weight also confounds capacity with substantially different accuracy losses.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite useful architectural and optimizer details. No implementation is linked, batch sizes and precise stopping criteria are missing, and independent training/attack repetitions are not specified. The reported visualization standard deviations do not establish stability across attack runs, which matters given the pronounced hyperparameter sensitivity.
